stem: A nurse employed by a hospital that is required to maintain OSHA injury and illness records sustains a work-related percutaneous injury from a hollow-bore needle contaminated with another person's blood. Which statement about federal OSHA recordkeeping is most accurate?

options.A: If source-patient testing is negative, the injury is not recorded because infection risk has been excluded.
options.B: The injury is recorded only if it later causes lost work time, restricted duty, or a diagnosed bloodborne infection.
options.C: Record the needlestick on the OSHA 300 Log as an injury while protecting the employee's identity, and maintain the required confidential sharps-injury information.
options.D: Keep the event only in employee-health records unless an occupational bloodborne infection is later diagnosed.

rationale: 29 CFR 1904.8 requires covered employers to record all work-related needlestick injuries and cuts from sharp objects contaminated with another person's blood or other potentially infectious material on the OSHA 300 Log as injuries. The employee's name is not entered because these are privacy-concern cases. Under 29 CFR 1910.1030(h)(5), employers required to maintain Part 1904 injury/illness logs must also establish and maintain a sharps-injury log containing specified device, work-area, and incident information in a manner that protects employee confidentiality. Recordability does not depend on source testing, lost work time, or a later infection diagnosis.
educational_objective: Apply federal OSHA recordkeeping rules by recording a work-related contaminated needlestick for a Part 1904-covered employer while protecting employee identity and maintaining confidential sharps-injury information.
source_document_title: 29 CFR 1904.8 — Recording criteria for needlestick and sharps injuries; 29 CFR 1910.1030(h)(5) — Sharps injury log
source_claim_supported: Section 1904.8(a) requires recording all work-related contaminated needlesticks/sharps injuries on OSHA 300 as injuries and protects identity; §1910.1030(h)(5) requires a confidential sharps-injury log for employers subject to Part 1904 recordkeeping.

source_original.stem: A nurse sustains a percutaneous injury from a blood-contaminated hollow-bore needle. Which statement about OSHA recordkeeping is most accurate?

options.A: If source testing is negative, treat the injury as nonrecordable under OSHA Part 1904 because infection risk has been excluded.
options.B: Record sharps injuries on the OSHA log when they cause lost work time or restricted duty, rather than when exposure alone occurs.
options.C: For Part 1904-covered employers, record the contaminated needlestick and maintain required sharps information while protecting confidentiality.
options.D: Keep the event in employee-health records but omit it from OSHA logs unless an occupational infection is later diagnosed.

source_original.rationale: OSHA requires work-related needlestick injuries from sharps contaminated with another person's blood or other potentially infectious material to be recorded when the employer is subject to Part 1904 recordkeeping. Such employers also maintain sharps-injury information while protecting employee confidentiality. Not every medical office is subject to the sharps-log requirement.
source_original.source_detail: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Quick Reference and 29 CFR 1904.8 — contaminated needlestick/sharps injuries are recordable for Part 1904-covered employers; sharps-injury information must protect confidentiality. Current OSHA federal requirements at exact URL; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control; Reporting of Incident/Event and infection/safety activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Added explicit Part 1904-covered-employer context to eliminate scope ambiguity. Tightened the key to distinguish the OSHA 300 privacy-concern entry from the separate sharps-injury log required by the Bloodborne Pathogens standard, and verified both requirements against current federal OSHA regulations.

audit_findings.exact_locator: 1904.8(a) controls contaminated-sharps recording/privacy; 1910.1030(h)(5) controls sharps-injury-log content/confidentiality/scope.
audit_findings.claim_audit: No claim depends on source-patient serology, seroconversion, or lost work time; those are explicitly not prerequisites for recording the contaminated needlestick.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because contaminated needlesticks are recorded regardless of later source test result.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because work restriction/lost time are not prerequisites for initial recording under 1904.8(a).
distractor_audit.C: Uniquely correct and captures both required records and confidentiality.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because the injury itself is recordable before any later infection diagnosis.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The revised stem removes employer-scope ambiguity; only C fits both Part 1904 and Bloodborne Pathogens recordkeeping rules.
audit_findings.cueing: All options concern timing/location of OSHA documentation; no unrelated clinical distractor.
audit_findings.blueprint: Maps to NCSBN incident/event and occupational safety reporting under Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Adversarial legal reread distinguished contaminated percutaneous injury from splash-only exposure and verified the privacy-concern rule; no unresolved scope conflict remains.
